title: Merge Sort
summary: Recursively split the input and merge sorted halves by choosing the smaller front value.
usage:
How it works
Ranges are half-open: [lo, hi). Recursively sort both halves, copy them, then write back their smallest remaining fronts. The merge invariant is that the written prefix is sorted. Useful when stable ordering and guaranteed running time matter. Temporary duplicates while writing back are normal; the copied halves retain the original values.

Properties and prerequisites
Stable: yes (choose the left value on ties). In-place: no in this implementation.

Complexity
Time: O(n log n) best/average/worst. Space: O(n) auxiliary + O(log n) stack.

Example
Input: [5, 2, 4, 1, 3]. Output: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5].

Try it
Use Play/Pause, Previous/Next, the timeline, and playback speed. Answer the prediction checkpoints to continue; feedback reveals the expected answer. Python is the line-synchronized walkthrough; Java is an equivalent complete implementation. Sorting functions accept empty arrays, duplicates, negative values, and already sorted inputs. Java methods belong inside a class; Python functions can be called directly.
pythonSource:
def merge_sort(a):
    def sort(lo, hi):
        if hi - lo <= 1:
            return
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2  # Split the half-open range [lo, hi).
        sort(lo, mid)
        sort(mid, hi)
        left, right = a[lo:mid], a[mid:hi]  # Copy the two sorted halves.
        i = j = 0
        k = lo
        while i < len(left) and j < len(right):
            if left[i] <= right[j]:  # Taking left on ties preserves stability.
                a[k] = left[i]
                i += 1
            else:
                a[k] = right[j]
                j += 1
            k += 1
        while i < len(left):
            a[k] = left[i]  # Copy the remaining left values.
            i += 1
            k += 1
        while j < len(right):
            a[k] = right[j]  # Copy the remaining right values.
            j += 1
            k += 1
    sort(0, len(a))
    return a
